The fallout of the board meeting moved with the terrifying speed of an avalanche. By Monday afternoon, the financial news networks were saturated with headlines detailing the arrest of Martin Sterling and Daniel Vance. Shares of Sterling Enterprises actually surged six percent upon the announcement that I was not only fully recovered but had proactively purged the corruption from my executive ranks.

Vanessa’s father called my office three separate times, begging for a private audience, while Vanessa herself had reportedly locked herself in her parents' penthouse, refusing to speak to the press. I didn't take their calls. I had my attorney handle the formal annulment of our engagement and the immediate repossession of the two-carat diamond ring I had foolishly placed on her finger months ago.

Back at the estate, the heavy, suffocating atmosphere of betrayal began to lift, replaced by a quiet reorganization of my life.

I dismissed half of the domestic staff—the sycophants and opportunists who had whispered behind my back and treated my supposed disability as a social inconvenience. But when it came to Clara, I made a very different decision.

"I'm promoting you," I said on Tuesday morning, standing in the bright, sunlit solarium as she watered the fiddle-leaf fig plants.

Clara paused, the brass watering can hovering over the soil. She turned around, looking genuinely alarmed. "Mr. Sterling, please... I'm just a housemaid. I don't know anything about corporate management or—"

"I'm not making you a vice president, Clara," I interrupted with a warm smile. "Though honestly, you'd probably run the logistics better than my uncle did. I want to appoint you as the head of household operations and my executive personal assistant."

She stared at me, dumbfounded. "Head of household? But what about Mrs. Higgins? She’s been here for twenty years."

"Mrs. Higgins was on Uncle Martin's payroll, leaking my daily schedule and dietary notes to my competitors," I replied bluntly, the warmth fading into cold reality. "She packed her bags this morning. You, on the other hand, have proven your loyalty where it actually counts. Unless... do you want to keep scrubbing baseboards?"

A slow, hesitant smile broke across Clara’s face, softening her features and making her look much younger than her twenty-four years. "I suppose I wouldn't mind trading the bleach for a proper desk."

"Good. It's settled."

Over the next two weeks, Clara transitioned into her new role with an instinctive grace and intelligence that continuously amazed me. She reorganized the estate’s chaotic administration in days, streamlined my personal schedule, and ensured that the vultures from our social circle were permanently barred from entering the gates.

For the first time since my father died, my home actually felt like a home.

Yet, as the crisp autumn air began to turn the leaves outside into vibrant shades of amber and gold, I realized that purging the corruption from my business and my house was only half the battle. The deeper wound—the lingering trauma of the assassination attempt and the profound loneliness of discovering everyone around me only loved my bank account—remained unhealed.

One evening, around 9:00 PM, I was working late in my private study. The desk was littered with merger proposals and legal briefs from the federal prosecutor’s office regarding Martin’s pending trial. A knock sounded at the heavy oak door.

"Come in," I muttered without looking up from my monitor.

The door clicked open, and light footsteps crossed the Persian rug. A steaming mug of chamomile tea was set gently beside my laptop, followed by a plate of warm, freshly baked cinnamon scones.

I looked up, expecting to see a caterer. Instead, it was Clara, wearing a simple cream-colored knit sweater and dark trousers, off-duty for the evening.

"You've been staring at those spreadsheets for four hours straight," Clara said softly, crossing her arms. "Even CEOs need sleep, Mr. Sterling."
